Stuart Beck and Estelle Ruellan, threat intelligence researchers at Flare, open by explaining how infostealer malware works. It harvests credentials, cookies and session data from an infected browser and uploads them to a collection server, where operators can retrieve them without further interaction. The team gathered stealer logs over a three-to-six month window and compared them against a pool of roughly 19,000 known command-and-control hosts, built from a C2 tracker export and from crawling pages similar to known infrastructure.

Five logs showed access to known C2 servers, spread across several countries and linked to different stealer families. One log stood out because its credentials were almost entirely tied to criminal activity rather than everyday accounts, which suggested the machine was used only for malicious purposes. Its access history pointed to administrative panels for several known malware families, including a multifunctional implant, a loader and a trojan. The researchers read this as a layered operation in which each tool supports the next, and they noted that the operator's own machine had been infected by another stealer.

The main takeaway is that stealer logs can serve as a practical source of infrastructure indicators, and that cybercriminals are not immune to the malware they distribute. In the Q&A, the speakers explained how they vet their sources and check whether harvested credentials still work, since repackaged combo lists can make stale data look valid.

talks.title: A Realistic Implementation
talks.teaser: Shows how a team turns vendor-neutral Sigma detection rules into SIEM queries through a git-based pipeline.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who works in incident response and detection, opens by explaining that Sigma is a generic YAML format for detection rules that can be shared and converted into queries for different SIEM and EDR platforms. Converting rules has become more practical with pySigma, which introduced backends that act as platform drivers and pipelines that map rules onto a specific environment's log sources and field names. The core problem raised is that stock Sigma rules often do not match real endpoint and SIEM data, and that maintaining rules by hand across many customer environments does not scale.

The middle of the talk covers the team's approach. Detection content lives in a git repository and is handled as code through a CI/CD workflow. Each change is validated against the Sigma specification, converted with Droid, a wrapper built on pySigma, and searched against existing datasets to surface false positives before export. Per-rule filters document accepted exclusions, a multi-tenant mode lets the same workflow reach several customer tenants, and a later integrity check compares deployed rules with the converted output. Branches move from feature to develop to main, which adds review at each stage. Unit testing with Atomic Red Team was described as work in progress.

The main takeaway is that detection logic can stay vendor-neutral, so changing a SIEM or EDR mainly means changing conversion settings rather than rewriting hundreds of rules. The speaker noted that the tool is open source and that correlation handling and more platforms remain open work. In the Q&A, run times were said to vary by platform because of API rate limits, and filtered alerts are still logged so analysts can revisit them later.

talks.title: Secrets In Squares - QR Codes
talks.teaser: Explores how sensitive information can be concealed within QR code images.

talks.title: Learn Anything
talks.teaser: Shares practical advice on learning new security skills, from repetition and learning styles to online communities and mentoring.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that learning stalls when the same explanation is repeated without changing its format. The speaker argues that repetition is useful, that people learn in different ways, and that a method that works for a friend may not work for you. Cost is not a reliable sign of quality, so free resources deserve the same attention as paid ones, and the advice is to try something, judge how it feels, and move on if it does not fit.

The middle section surveys the ways people learn today. Online platforms now offer beginner-friendly material on subjects such as AI, where only university-level mathematical content existed a few years ago, and some courses offer certificates. Communities, forums, chats, meetups and conferences give access to people who can answer questions, while video platforms and blogs offer another route, with comments and feedback as a way to engage with the people who make the content.

The closing point is mentoring. Asking an experienced person to explain something, or to review a personal project, often turns into an informal mentoring relationship. That arrangement adds accountability, which the speaker found valuable. The takeaway is to start now, accept that early attempts may fall short, and keep trying different methods until one fits.

talks.title: Luks Full Disk Encryption Upside-Down
talks.teaser: Takes a five-minute look at LUKS full disk encryption from an upside-down angle on the topic.

talks.title: Pentests Using LLMs
talks.teaser: Surveys how offensive AI and large language models could automate parts of penetration testing and attacker tradecraft.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a broad look at artificial intelligence in cyber security. The speaker argues that AI is a flexible base for building security tools and that the field is changing quickly enough to matter now. The discussion focuses on offensive use, and the speaker also raises the risks that more pessimistic views of machine intelligence point to.

The core of the talk sorts offensive AI into five areas: social engineering with deepfakes and phishing, evading detection with polymorphic malware, reconnaissance through open-source intelligence and automated target discovery, credential attacks against biometric systems, and automated exploit development, including malware co-pilots. The argument is that a large share of common attacker tactics could be automated or sped up with language models, which would make them cheaper to run. The open-source PentestGPT project was cited as an existing example, alongside a proprietary project still in development.

The speaker then covered the challenges: ethical concerns, false positives, and the reliability of model output. The need for more targeted exploit generation, so defenders can test their own systems and build countermeasures, was also raised. The talk noted that AI models have their own weaknesses, such as prompt injection and training data poisoning. The closing takeaway is that the industry should take a responsible and strategic approach so defenders can prepare for these capabilities.

talks.title: Internal Domain Name Collision 2.0
talks.teaser: Shows how leaked internal domain names can be registered to capture misdirected traffic from corporate networks.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with a red team engagement in which an external Exchange server leaked an internal NTLM domain name ending in .llc. That suffix had become a public top-level domain in 2018 and was still available to buy. Registering it and running a DNS server captured internal lookups, including WPAD and Active Directory discovery queries from workstations. The team then used the harvested domain credentials to reach the VPN, where the client's push-approval MFA was approved by a user.

The speaker explains name collisions: when new top-level domains are delegated while internal networks still use the same suffixes, lookups leak to the internet. ICANN's collision framework proposes a short interception period, but the speaker argues it mainly serves the registry's revenue. The research method gathered internal names from certificates, SMTP banners, email headers and NTLM challenges, then checked registration status through DNS records and registrar APIs, since WHOIS checks got the team blocked. Case studies included a Memphis police domain tied to a real-time crime center, the .ad domain, a blockchain .box TLD where router default suffixes leaked traffic, and Luxembourg, where hundreds of unregistered domains were tied to municipalities, a school and a bank.

The main takeaway is that organizations should register or sinkhole any internal-looking domain names they use, and reduce reliance on WPAD and unqualified internal names. The research reported about 89,000 unregistered domains, roughly 115 of which were registered, and hundreds of millions of DNS records captured over six months.

talks.title: Reverse Engineering Android Apps With ACVTool
talks.teaser: Shows how the ACVTool coverage tool helps reverse engineer Android apps by stripping out code that never runs.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why reverse engineering modern Android apps is hard, since large commercial packages ship with many dex files, split APKs and heavily obfuscated bytecode. It starts with how Android packages are structured and with the usual tooling around decompilers, disassemblers and proxies.

The main focus is ACVTool, a tool first developed at the University of Luxembourg to measure code coverage for apps without source code. The updated 2024 version supports multi-dex apps, swaps APKTool for a lighter repackaging step so manifests and resources are less likely to break, and can measure coverage of a single feature. The app is instrumented, exercised on a device or emulator, and the collected coverage is turned into an HTML report. Two examples are shown: a Firebase login app the speaker wrote, where about 6% of the code remained after shrinking away unused classes, and a dice-rolling app analysed by building a graph of executed methods from entry points such as click and sensor handlers.

The takeaway is that runtime coverage can narrow down what to read in a large decompiled app. The shrinking technique is still experimental and fails on many applications, so it is best treated as an aid for focusing analysis on the code that actually executes.

talks.title: Detection And Response For Linux Without EDR
talks.teaser: Explains how Linux detection and response can work with auditd-based logging and open tooling instead of a commercial EDR.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who runs detection engineering for a logistics company's fleet of more than 10,000 Linux servers, starts from a practical problem: standard system logs miss most attacker activity, including web shells, reverse shells and rootkits. Raw Linux audit records are hard to use at scale because their values are hex-encoded and each event spans several lines, which makes them awkward for a SIEM to parse.

To address this, the team built Laurel, an open-source plugin that consumes audit output and merges each event into structured JSON lines. It adds process parent-child tracking, process labeling to reduce false positives in busy enterprise environments, and captures selected environment variables to spot user-space preload rootkits. The talk also covers why the team evaluated commercial EDR products and dropped them, citing Windows-oriented designs that mishandled Linux concepts such as numeric user IDs and non-Unicode filenames. For response, the team adopted Velociraptor to run live queries like process and network listings without relying on tools on the host that could be compromised.

The closing discussion covered performance, where the speaker said Laurel compared favorably with auditd and Sysmon for Linux in synthetic process-spawn tests. Questions also touched on eBPF, which the team has not adopted yet because of older kernels in long-support enterprise systems. The takeaway is that a well-configured audit subsystem, with its output structured and enriched properly, can deliver useful detection coverage without an EDR agent.

talks.title: Mapping The Information System
talks.teaser: Explains how an organisation's information system can be mapped to show its components and the links between them.

talks.title: Disconnecting Games With A Single Packet: An Unreal Untold Story
talks.teaser: Shows how one crafted UDP packet can force players in Unreal Engine games to disconnect.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a denial-of-service weakness in Unreal Engine, a widely used game engine whose source code can be inspected publicly. The presenter explains why cheating is a major concern for the games industry and why the network layer, which every client and server depends on, is a useful target. Unreal's application-layer protocol runs over UDP, and the game server identifies each client only by its IP address and port. When an incoming packet fails the engine's sanity checks, the engine disconnects the associated player instead of simply discarding the packet.

Using static analysis of the engine code and profiling of a simple test game, the researchers identified five ways to craft packets that fail these checks without needing any knowledge of earlier traffic. Payload encryption does not stop this, because the fields that trigger the disconnect sit in the header, which stays unencrypted. Two demonstrations were shown: a Valorant match where a defender was repeatedly disconnected while the bomb was planted, and a Fortnite scenario where a peer-to-peer call over the PlayStation Network exposed an opponent's address.

The speaker then covered how an attacker could reach a target: broadcasting on a shared local network, spoofing source addresses from networks that do not validate them, and brute-forcing the port behind a firewall, which can take only seconds at modest rates. Suggested mitigations include encrypting the full packet, dropping rather than disconnecting on failed checks, and using TLS or DTLS. The vendor treated the report as informative and did not fix the issue, so the speaker urged studios to modify the engine source themselves.
